routes.description: Establish that biblical truth is properly assessed through genre, revelation, human testimony, and established interpretive tradition, and that textual variation or morally difficult passages need not defeat its historical, theological, moral, or revelatory claims.
routes.successCriteria: Connect an account of revelation and human transmission to affirmative historical or cosmological support, while explaining why apparent contradictions and difficult moral texts do not undermine the Bible's governing truth claims.

motionBridge.description: Show that the Bible remains true in its governing revelatory and theological purpose while retaining sufficient historical and moral credibility across its diverse genres.

centralBridges.description: Define biblical truth through revelation, genre, authorial purpose, and human expression rather than requiring uniform literal or scientific precision.
Establish that cumulative testimony and external corroboration support the historical credibility of the biblical narratives despite nonidentical details.
Explain morally troubling texts through moral development, fulfillment, and the established interpretive practice of living Christian communities.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use claimed convergence between Genesis and later cosmological inquiry as supporting evidence for revelation.
Distinguish ordinary testimonial variation from central falsification and explain why miraculous claims remain possible within the asserted theology.

routes.description: Establish that each biblical claim must meet standards appropriate to its genre and that historical contradictions, theological reshaping, selective evidential methods, and morally troubling divine commands undermine the Bible's asserted forms of truth.
routes.successCriteria: Demonstrate that the principal historical, revelatory, and moral claims face unresolved contradictions or counterexamples that cannot be answered merely by invoking genre, possibility, later tradition, or beneficial reception.

motionBridge.description: Show that contradictions and morally troubling texts materially undermine the Bible's historical, moral, theological, allegorical, or revelatory truth claims.

centralBridges.description: Separate the Bible's genres and require attempted historical reports, moral teachings, and allegories to satisfy the standards appropriate to each claim.
Show that Gospel discrepancies, textual development, and theological reshaping reduce confidence in the narratives used to support central Christian events.
Show that divinely authorized killing and slavery remain incompatible with asserted biblical moral authority despite later reinterpretation or moral development.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require consistent treatment of favorable and unfavorable scientific, archaeological, and textual details when inferring revelation or reliability.
Distinguish the logical possibility of miracles from evidence that specifically biblical miracle reports occurred.

sections.title: Standards of Truth, Genre, and Revelation
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the governing standards for evaluating a diverse scriptural library, including the roles of authorial purpose, human expression, revelation, allegory, and inherited interpretation.

sections.title: Gospel Historicity, Contradictions, and Transmission
sections.rationale: The historical reliability of the Gospels is a principal motion-level clash because discrepancies, editorial development, cumulative testimony, and theological shaping bear directly on central Christian events.

sections.title: Cosmology, Archaeological Corroboration, and Miracles
sections.rationale: Affirmative appeals to scientific anticipation, archaeological detail, and miraculous possibility must be weighed against alternative explanations and limits on what mundane corroboration can establish.

sections.title: Divine Violence and Biblical Moral Authority
sections.rationale: Commands involving conquest and the killing of noncombatants create a direct test of claimed divine moral authority and of whether development, fulfillment, or interpretive tradition resolves difficult texts.

sections.title: Slavery, Moral Development, and Abolitionist Reception
sections.rationale: Biblical slave laws, later teachings, abolitionist use, and communal interpretation test whether the canon presents coherent moral development or contains unresolved moral instability.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Because the Bible is a library containing diverse genres, its literal, historical, allegorical, moral, theological, and metaphorical truth claims must be examined separately.
moves.attributionBasis: The announced opening order and sustained first-person framing identify Alex O'Connor as the speaker throughout this passage.
